title: Tesla drops 'Full Self-Driving' brand name in Europe after regulator pushback
content: Elon Musk 's automaker Tesla has changed the brand name of its "Full Self-Driving (Supervised)," or FSD, system in Europe to "Assisted Driving" after German regulators called the branding "somewhat misleading." The package is still sold under the Full Self-Driving (Supervised) branding in the U.S. as a $99 per month subscription for Tesla owners. Tesla is gunning for approvals across Europe, where EV sales have been on the rise this year amid soaring fuel costs caused by the war in Iran, and where Tesla sales have shown signs of recovery from a sales slump last year. On Tuesday, the German Federal Ministry of Transport , known as the BMV, said in a statement that Tesla's brand name "FSD" was "somewhat misleading," adding that "It is not a system that takes over the entire driving task. Rather, it is a driver assistance system that can support certain driving tasks such as accelerating, braking, and steering. The driver must remain attentive at all times." Tesla has been pressuring automotive regulators in Europe, especially in the Netherlands, for rapid approval of their system. Reuters reported that in some cases, Tesla's " browbeating " pushed regulators to reduce the intensity of their safety tests and reviews of the company's technology. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, the U.S. automotive safety regulator, is also investigating Tesla's FSD to determine if it is safe for drivers to use in fog, glaring sun or other reduced visibility conditions, and is investigating Tesla to determine whether FSD caused Tesla drivers to commit traffic violations — some that resulted in collisions. In December 2025, a judge in California determined that Tesla had engaged in deceptive marketing around its Autopilot and FSD systems, falsely implying they were fully automated driving systems. Tesla has countersued the California DMV to try to shed that "false advertiser" label in a Los Angeles superior court. That litigation is ongoing. Autonomous systems expert Missy Cummings, an engineering professor at George Mason University and outspoken critic of Tesla and other autonomous vehicle developers, said renaming FSD isn't a strong enough measure to ensure the systems are safe for broad release in Europe. In an email to CNBC, Cummings said European agencies are "ignoring both past and ongoing NHTSA investigations" into safety defects with Tesla's FSD. "The EU is struggling to keep up in the AI marketplace," she said. "Musk sees this and is definitely bullying them as a result." She criticized the Dutch regulator, known as RDW, for approving Tesla FSD for release in Europe, "based on secretive data," adding that, "The public should demand transparency in any approval of a transportation system with embedded AI." Tesla and RDW did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In its second-quarter earnings update, Tesla said it had 1.48 million "active" FSD subscriptions but did not say how many were activated from free trials or other incentives.

A study of twisted two-dimensional semiconductors reveals how subtle material disorder can emerge at different spatial scales. Two distinct forms of hidden disorder may influence how ultrathin semiconductors emit light. One extends across relatively large areas of the material, while the other is concentrated around tiny defects. A new theoretical approach offers a way to identify these patterns by analyzing changes in light emission rather than attempting to separate individual spectral signals. Developed by Katsunori Wakabayashi at the Research Center for Materials Nanoarchitectonics (MANA), part of the National Institute for Materials Science (NIMS), the framework could provide a more reliable way to investigate imperfections in materials used for advanced optical and quantum devices. The research examines moiré heterostructures, which form when two extremely thin semiconductor layers are stacked with a slight rotational misalignment. In materials such as molybdenum diselenide and tungsten diselenide (MoSe2/WSe2), this arrangement creates a repeating moiré pattern that alters how the combined layers interact with and emit light. These structures produce complex photoluminescence spectra containing numerous overlapping emission peaks. Scientists typically study such spectra by identifying individual peaks and determining their physical origins. However, the dense, overlapping signals in moiré heterostructures make those assignments difficult and potentially uncertain. Wakabayashi developed a mathematical framework that examines how simpler spectral properties, including peak energy and average emission energy, change across a material’s surface. Applying the approach to previously reported spectral correlations in a MoSe2/WSe2 heterostructure suggested that different optical features respond to different scales of structural disorder. The analysis identified two possible components of this hidden disorder. The first is a smoothly varying ‘background’ extending over distances of a few micrometers (roughly 0.0001 inch). The second is much more localized and may arise from small defects or sites where excitons become trapped. Excitons are bound pairs of electrons and positively charged holes that can release energy as light. By comparing spatial variations in the spectral measurements with theoretical predictions, the framework makes it possible to infer the underlying disorder without assigning an origin to every emission peak. This approach could eventually help researchers evaluate material quality and improve the consistency of semiconductor manufacturing. “This work could help researchers make better and more reproducible materials for light-emitting devices, optical sensors, and quantum technologies,” remarks Wakabayashi. Reference: “Hierarchical disorder in moiré exciton photoluminescence probed by spectral-descriptor correlations” by Katsunori Wakabayashi, 7 August 2026, Physical Review Research . title: Prize-winning image which sparked backlash was AI-generated, Nikon rules
content:
The winner of a prestigious scientific photography competition has been disqualified following concerns raised by other scientists that it was fake.
Nikon said the use of generative AI in the composition of the video broke the rules of its Small World In Motion contest, which accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes.
The firm said the video "did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI", but added it was not a judgement of the entrant's professional reputation or scientific contributions.
It said it would now look at the rules and procedures of the annual contest, which has been running for 15 years and is specifically for microscopic images.
Nikon said it came to the decision "after thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel".
The winning entry came from Dr Ning Xu, from Tsinghua University in China, who submitted a short video showing tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving in the airway of a child with the respiratory condition PCD.
The BBC has approached him for comment.
A number of scientists, including former competition judges, complained to Nikon on its LinkedIn page that the video did not appear to be real.
Xu had acknowledged using AI, but said he believed he had acted within the rules, and had cooperated with Nikon's investigation.
University of Leicester scientist Dr Robert Hirst, who was among the first experts to voice concerns, said he was "not surprised" and he "knew immediately that the video was fabricated".
"I have been diagnosing PCD for 20 years by examining their cilia waveform, length, cell size and shape," he said.
Hirst, who is lead scientist for the NHS centre for PCD diagnosis at the university, said the cells and cilia "look nothing like those from PCD patients".
"This controversy has impacted a lot of patients, scientists, doctors and PCD support networks around the world," he said.

title: Anthropic bans users from being 'cruel' to its AI systems
content:
Anthropic has raised eyebrows by announcing it will ban users from "sustained and needless" abusive behaviour towards its AI.
The Claude-maker said on Thursday it was updating its usage policy to let its tools end interactions where people are "cruel" - something it said it had done in "rare" cases prior.
It will now be included on a list of forbidden conduct which also contains bullying others, promoting self-harm and creating non-consensual intimate imagery.
While Anthropic said the policy would only apply in "extreme cases" of repeated abuse, it has reignited debate over how we should communicate with AI tools.
The company said it would not apply to "common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research" - suggesting it would only apply in clearly deliberate instances.
But what Anthropic would consider "abusive or cruel behaviour" towards its models remains unclear.
Screenshots of the new policy have been widely shared and commented on across social media - with some praising it as advancing good manners or "model welfare".
But others criticised the plan, with one person calling it " deeply wrong " and another suggesting it might undermine abuse directed at humans and animals.
"You can't be cruel to numbers and maths," wrote Dr Barry Scannell, technology partner at Irish law firm William Fry, on LinkedIn .
"This level of anthropomorphisation of AI is harmful. It leads people to believe that it's something it's not."
Microsoft AI director Mustafa Suleyman, who in September criticised rival firm Anthropic for treating AI like it is human , reacted to Anthropic's update with a melting face emoji.
The changes, first reported by tech outlet The Verge, came following an annual review of the usage policy at the firm.
It was also updated to address new or emerging risks in other areas, including by forbidding use of Claude for "deceptive campaigns" or clarifying that, as US midterm elections loom , it cannot be used to "deceive voters or disrupt elections".
Anthropic also said on Thursday its usage policy previously prevented its tools being used to develop weapons.
But none of the updates have attracted as much attention or scrutiny as its move to forbid users abusing its chatbots.
It has also tapped into the much-debated question of whether we should be curt or polite when using generative AI tools.
Some experts say writing or saying "please" or "thank you" to tools like ChatGPT is unnecessary and wastes tokens - used by the large language models powering generative AI tools to process and reply to you.
Others argue politeness can lead to higher quality answers or responses.
When a X user last year asked about electricity costs incurred by ChatGPT replying to users' "please" and "thank you" messages, OpenAI boss Sam Altman said it was "tens of millions of dollars well spent - you never know".
The Collins Dictionary meanwhile last November highlighted the re-emergence of the term "clanker" for disparagingly referring to AI tools .

title: Police trial AI chatbot to free up call handlers
content:
Staffordshire Police has launched an AI-powered chatbot to answer non-emergency queries from people, in a bid to cut waiting times and free up call handlers for more complex cases.
The force claimed it was the first in the West Midlands to introduce Bobbi, an AI-virtual assistant, available through the live chat function on its website.
Ch Supt Matthew Morgan, head of the force's contact centre, said one of the most common questions from the public was whether an incident was a crime.
Bobbi is designed to provide answers to routine inquiries, alongside existing online forms, telephone lines and front counters.
"It's designed to make it as easy and as fast as possible to get people answers to common questions," Morgan added.
The force said the chatbot had undergone "robust and relentless challenges" before being launched for a 12-month trial period.
"We wouldn't have deployed it otherwise," Morgan said.
The technology has already been trialled by a number of other forces, including Merseyside Police , Thames Valley Police and Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary.
Staffordshire Police said Bobbi would not replace human call handlers, but help reduce demand on the contact centre.
"Ultimately, what it does is free up our call handlers to focus on those complex and urgent inquiries that absolutely 100% necessitate a human agent," Ch Supt Morgan said.
Bobbi cannot be used to report crimes and is not replacing the 999 emergency service, the force said. Complex or sensitive inquiries will also continue to be dealt with by human staff.

title: 'Careless use of AI is the real threat - not the ghost stories'
content:
Warning: This article contains strong language.
Meredith Whittaker has little patience for the AI doom that dominates headlines - she thinks warnings of AI turning on humanity is a fear "not anchored in science".
"The risk is very real," says the boss of the Signal Foundation, which runs the encrypted messaging app of the same name, "but it's not the shiny ghost stories the wild-eyed boys are talking about".
Instead, she believes the more immediate danger is the technology being used carelessly.
She cites an alleged incident, reported by CNN, in which a chatbot used by US intelligence invented information about a Chinese vessel carrying nuclear material, reportedly leading the US to prepare a military response.
"We almost went to war with China," she tells BBC Global Women.
"A system that produces faulty intelligence and almost gets us into a war with China should not be considered super-intelligent by any standards."
Signal has an estimated 40-70 million users - a drop in the ocean next to WhatsApp, which has billions.
But it is renowned for its tough stance on protecting users' privacy - it hides who is sending a message from its own servers, limiting the data available to outside observers or hackers.
Time magazine named Whittaker one of the most powerful people in AI. She moves through the rooms where its future is discussed, from Silicon Valley boardrooms to Downing Street, Davos and the Vatican.
She studied literature at university and joined Google in 2006 as an entry-level temp with no computer science degree.
In late 2017, she made her name when a colleague told her about Project Maven, a secret Google contract with the US Department of Defense to build AI for drone targeting.
She understood what it meant to "compress the kill chain": to shrink the time between a machine flagging a target and someone deciding to fire, reducing deliberation. With thousands of colleagues, she pushed back.
"This is going to launder bad intelligence and bad data," she remembers arguing publicly.
The following year Whittaker helped organise a walkout, in which some 20,000 staff protested against the company's handling of several issues, including what they felt was the rushed introduction of new technology. Google dropped the contract and Palantir picked it up.
She draws a direct line from Maven to the US missile attack on a school in Iran this year, which she says relied on the system and on outdated intelligence that identified the school as a military target.
"This is exactly what we were warning about in 2017," she says.
In response, Palantir told Global Women there was "no evidence that Palantir's software was at fault in this terrible tragedy".
It added that "Palantir is not responsible for the underlying data nor identifying intelligence deficiencies". And earlier this year it's UK and Europe boss, Louis Mosley told the BBC that "there's always a human in the loop, so there is always a human that makes the ultimate decision".
The US military has yet to release the findings of its investigation into the Minab strike, but Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said it would "never target civilian targets".
